text: Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor. Yet th[ey] support rou[ghly] a quarter o[f] all mar[ine] species. T[he] reason i[s] that cor[als] build intr[icate] structures, wh[ich] provide she[lter] for fish, shrimp, and many other creatures. Tiny algae live inside coral tissue and supply most of the energy the animals need. When the water becomes too warm, the corals expel these algae, turn white, and may eventually starve if conditions do not improve quickly. Because reefs also protect coastlines from storm waves, their decline affects millions of people.

Volcanic islands are born when magma rises through the ocean crust and piles up on the seafloor. Over thou[sands] of ye[ars], repeated erup[tions] build a moun[tain] that fin[ally] breaks t[he] surface o[f] the oc[ean]. After t[he] volcano bec[omes] inactive, erosion slowly wears the island down, while the heavy rock beneath sinks under its own weight. Eventually only a ring of coral may remain, enclosing a shallow lagoon where the mountain once stood.

The printing press changed European society in less than a century. Before i[ts] invention, bo[oks] were cop[ied] by ha[nd], so th[ey] were expe[nsive] and ra[re]. Once pre[sses] could ma[ke] hundreds o[f] identical pages quickly, prices dropped sharply and literacy began to spread beyond the clergy. New ideas travelled faster than authorities could suppress them, which helped fuel religious reform and scientific debate across the continent. Governments soon began to regulate what could be printed.

Memory is not a perfect recording of past events. Instead, peo[ple] reconstruct exper[iences] each ti[me] they rec[all] them, fil[ling] in mis[sing] details wi[th] assumptions a[nd] later infor[mation]. This pro[cess] explains why two witnesses of the same accident can give different accounts, and why confident memories are sometimes wrong. Researchers have shown that even a small change in the wording of a question can alter what a person remembers. Courts now treat eyewitness testimony with greater caution.

Inflation describes a general rise in prices over time. When i[t] is l[ow] and ste[ady], businesses c[an] plan inves[tments] with reaso[nable] confidence. How[ever], rapid infl[ation] erodes t[he] value o[f] savings and makes wages harder to negotiate. Central banks therefore try to control it by adjusting interest rates, which influence how much people borrow and spend. Raising rates usually slows price growth, but it can also reduce hiring and economic activity. Policymakers must balance these risks carefully.

Exoplanets are planets that orbit stars other than our Sun. Because th[ey] are extr[emely] faint comp[ared] with t[he] stars th[ey] circle, astro[nomers] rarely s[ee] them dire[ctly]. Instead, th[ey] often det[ect] a planet by measuring the slight dimming of starlight when it passes in front of its star. Repeated dimming at regular intervals reveals the orbit of the planet, and the amount of dimming indicates its approximate size. Larger telescopes are now revealing thousands of such worlds.

Impressionist painters broke with tradition by working outdoors and capturing fleeting effects of light. Rather th[an] blending col[ors] smoothly, th[ey] applied th[ick], visible brushs[trokes] that see[med] rough t[o] critics a[t] the ti[me]. Their subj[ects] were also unusual, since they preferred everyday scenes such as train stations, gardens, and crowded cafes over historical or religious themes. Audiences gradually accepted this approach, and it eventually influenced almost every later movement. Today their paintings are among the most popular in the world.

Languages change constantly, although speakers rarely notice the process while it is happening. Pronunciation shi[fts] gradually, n[ew] words app[ear], and o[ld] grammatical patt[erns] fade fr[om] use. Ling[uists] compare rel[ated] languages t[o] reconstruct ance[stors] that left no written records. For example, similar words for water and mother across many European and Asian languages suggest that they share a common origin thousands of years ago. Such comparisons are among the most powerful tools in historical linguistics.

Wetlands act as natural filters for the water that flows through them. Dense pla[nts] slow t[he] current, allo[wing] soil part[icles] to set[tle], while microor[ganisms] break do[wn] many pollu[tants]. Wetlands al[so] absorb exc[ess] rainfall, which reduces the risk of flooding in nearby towns. Despite these benefits, large areas have been drained for farming and construction, and scientists warn that the loss of wetlands is difficult to reverse. Restoration projects exist, but they are costly and slow.

Many birds travel thousands of kilometers each year between breeding and wintering grounds. Scientists on[ce] assumed th[at] they rel[ied] only o[n] landmarks, b[ut] experiments ha[ve] revealed a mo[re] complex pic[ture]. Birds app[ear] to se[nse] the magnetic field of the Earth, and they also use the position of the sun and stars. Young birds migrating for the first time often follow instinct, whereas experienced adults refine their routes through memory. Some species even return to the same nest each year.

The Moon is slowly moving away from the Earth at about four centimeters per year. This hap[pens] because ti[des] raise bul[ges] of wa[ter] on t[he] planet, a[nd] friction dr[ags] these bul[ges] slightly ah[ead] of t[he] Moon. The gravity of the bulges pulls the Moon forward, which gradually enlarges its orbit. At the same time, the rotation of the Earth slows, so days were noticeably shorter in the distant past. Fossil records of ancient corals support this conclusion.

Trade routes such as the Silk Road carried far more than goods. Merchants exch[anged] religious bel[iefs], technologies, a[nd] even dise[ases] as th[ey] crossed des[erts] and moun[tains]. Cities al[ong] the rou[tes] grew wea[lthy] by taxing caravans and offering lodging to travelers. When sea travel later became cheaper and safer, overland trade declined, and many of these cities lost their former importance. Today only ruins remain in some of them, though archaeologists still find coins and pottery there.

Sleep is essential for learning, yet many students sacrifice it before examinations. During de[ep] sleep, t[he] brain rehe[arses] recent exper[iences] and stren[gthens] the conne[ctions] that st[ore] them. Resea[rchers] have fo[und] that peo[ple] who sleep after studying remember more than those who stay awake for the same period. Consequently, an all-night study session can be less effective than a shorter review followed by a full night of rest. Schools are slowly beginning to share this advice with students.

Glaciers shape landscapes through the slow movement of enormous masses of ice. As a gla[cier] advances, i[t] picks u[p] rocks a[nd] drags th[em] along t[he] valley fl[oor], carving de[ep] U-shaped val[leys]. When t[he] ice finally melts, it leaves behind piles of debris called moraines, as well as lakes that fill the hollows it created. These features allow geologists to reconstruct where ice once existed. Many famous lakes and fjords originated in exactly this way.

title: Tardigrades: Survivors of Drought
text:
Tardigrades, often called water bears, are microscopic animals less than a millimeter long. They live almost everywhere, from mountain moss to deep ocean sediment, and they are famous for surviving conditions that would kill most other creatures. When their environment dries out, tardigrades curl into a dry, shriveled form known as a tun. In this state their metabolism falls to a tiny fraction of its normal rate, and they can remain dormant for years. Once water returns, they swell and resume moving within hours.

Scientists have long wondered how tardigrades protect their cells during drying. One discovery was that they produce special proteins that form a glass-like substance inside their cells, preventing delicate structures from collapsing. This is different from the strategy of many other organisms, which rely on sugars for protection. Researchers hope that these proteins might one day help preserve medicines and vaccines without refrigeration.

Despite their reputation, tardigrades are not indestructible. They survive extreme dryness and radiation, but prolonged heat above a certain level still kills them, and they cannot reproduce while in the dormant state.

A sugar used to protect cells
qs.explain: The passage defines a tun as the dry, shriveled form of a tardigrade.

qs.explain: Dormant here means inactive: metabolism is almost stopped for years.

choices: They form a glass-like substance that prevents structures from collapsing
They lower the animal's body temperature
qs.explain: The proteins form a glass-like substance; sugars are the strategy of other organisms.

To explain how tardigrades were discovered
To argue that refrigeration is harmful
To suggest a possible practical use of the research

title: Wegener and Moving Continents
text:
When Alfred Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents were once joined and had slowly drifted apart, most geologists rejected the idea. Wegener pointed to the matching shapes of South America and Africa, as well as identical fossils of land animals found on continents now separated by thousands of kilometers. Critics did not dispute these observations; they objected that he could not explain what force could push continents through solid ocean floor. His suggestion that tides or the rotation of the planet were responsible was quickly shown to be far too weak.

The debate shifted only decades later, when mapping of the seafloor revealed long mountain ridges running through the middle of oceans. Rock samples showed that the crust is youngest at the ridges and grows progressively older with distance, indicating that new crust forms there and spreads outward. Magnetic stripes in the rock, which record reversals of Earth's magnetic field, appeared in mirror-image patterns on either side of the ridges, strongly supporting the idea.

Thus Wegener was right that continents move, but the mechanism turned out to be seafloor spreading rather than continents plowing through the ocean floor. His central observation was eventually vindicated even though his explanation was not.

qs.q: Why did most geologists reject Wegener's idea in 1912?
choices: His fossil evidence was shown to be false
The continents clearly did not fit together
He could not explain a force strong enough to move continents
qs.explain: Critics accepted his observations but objected that he had no adequate mechanism.

qs.q: The word "dispute" in the passage is closest in meaning to
qs.explain: Critics did not challenge the observations; their objection was about the cause.

qs.q: Why does the author mention magnetic stripes?
choices: To show that Earth's magnetic field never changes
As evidence that new crust forms at ridges and spreads outward
To explain why fossils match across oceans
To prove that tides move continents
qs.explain: The mirror-image stripes on both sides of ridges support seafloor spreading.

qs.q: What can be inferred about the acceptance of continental drift?
choices: It depended on evidence that was unavailable in Wegener's time
It was accepted immediately by most geologists
It was based on Wegener's explanation of tides
It required the rejection of seafloor spreading
qs.explain: Acceptance followed seafloor mapping decades later, which Wegener could not have used.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Wegener's theory of tides explained continental movement
Fossils alone proved that continents drift
Wegener's claim that continents move was eventually supported, though his proposed cause was wrong
Seafloor spreading disproved the idea that continents move
qs.explain: The last paragraph states his central observation was vindicated but his explanation was not.

title: The Hanseatic League
text:
In the late Middle Ages, a network of merchant towns around the Baltic and North Seas formed an association known as the Hanseatic League. No single ruler governed it. Instead, towns such as Lubeck, Hamburg, and Bruges sent representatives to occasional assemblies, where they agreed on common rules for trade and mutual defense. Members benefited from reduced tolls and protection against pirates, and merchants from the League could operate in foreign ports with privileges that outsiders lacked.

The League's power rested largely on its control of bulk goods such as timber, grain, fish, and furs. Salted herring was especially important, because it could feed populations far from the coast during religious fasting periods. When a city broke the League's rules, the other members could impose a trade boycott, which was often more effective than military force. On rare occasions the League did go to war, as in the conflict with the Danish crown in the fourteenth century.

The League declined in the sixteenth century. Stronger national states began to favor their own merchants, and the discovery of Atlantic trade routes shifted commerce away from the Baltic. By the seventeenth century only a few cities still took part in its assemblies.

qs.q: How was the Hanseatic League governed?
choices: By assemblies of representatives from member towns
qs.explain: No single ruler governed it; towns sent representatives to occasional assemblies.

qs.explain: Privileges that outsiders lacked are special advantages.

qs.q: Why does the author mention salted herring?
choices: To show that fishing replaced timber trading
To explain why the League went to war
To argue that the League ignored religion
To illustrate a bulk good for which demand was strong
qs.explain: Herring is given as an especially important bulk good because it fed distant populations during fasting.

qs.q: Which of the following can be inferred about a trade boycott?
choices: It was never used by the League
It was weaker than military force
It was effective because members depended on League trade
qs.explain: The passage says boycotts were often more effective than force, implying cities could not afford to lose League trade.

qs.explain: Tolls, pirate protection and port privileges are listed; guaranteed prices are never mentioned.

title: Hedonic Adaptation
text:
Psychologists use the term hedonic adaptation to describe the tendency of people to return to a stable level of happiness after major positive or negative events. In a frequently cited study, researchers compared lottery winners with people who had been paralyzed in accidents. Within a year or so, the winners were not substantially happier than before, and the accident victims reported more happiness than most observers would have predicted.

Some scholars argue that this finding has been overstated. Later research using larger samples that followed individuals for many years showed that adaptation is incomplete: bereavement, long-term unemployment, and chronic pain can lower well-being for years, and people do not always recover to their earlier baseline. Moreover, adaptation seems to vary with the type of event. People adjust quickly to purchases and improved living conditions, but they adapt more slowly to ongoing sources of stress, such as a long commute or a noisy neighborhood, because these demands return every day.

The concept nonetheless has practical value. It suggests that people often overestimate how long their emotional reactions to future events will last, a bias that can lead them to pursue wealth or status at the expense of activities that continue to provide enjoyment over time.

qs.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: People tend to adapt emotionally to events, but adaptation is neither complete nor uniform
People always return to the same happiness level after any event
Lottery winners are less happy than accident victims
Stress cannot be reduced by changing one's environment
qs.explain: The passage presents the adaptation idea and then shows later research limiting it.

qs.q: The word "overstated" in the passage is closest in meaning to
qs.explain: Saying a finding was overstated means it was exaggerated.

qs.q: Why does the author mention a long commute?
choices: To show that purchases bring lasting happiness
To give an example of a stressor that people adapt to slowly
To explain why lottery winners stay happy
To illustrate a one-time negative event
qs.explain: The commute is an ongoing stressor that returns daily, so adaptation is slower.

qs.q: What does the passage suggest about the original lottery study?
choices: Its conclusion applies less universally than often claimed
It used larger samples than later studies
It showed accident victims became happier than winners
qs.explain: Later work found adaptation incomplete and event-dependent, so the early finding was too general, though not entirely false.

qs.q: According to the passage, adaptation is slower for which kind of event?
choices: Ongoing stressors that recur every day
qs.explain: Purchases and better living conditions bring quick adaptation; daily recurring stressors are adapted to slowly.

title: Comparative Advantage
text:
Economists have long argued that countries benefit from trade even when one of them can produce everything more efficiently than the other. The explanation lies in the concept of comparative advantage. Consider a country that can produce either wheat or cloth. If it gives up a small amount of cloth for each additional unit of wheat, it has a comparative advantage in wheat, even if another country can grow wheat with fewer workers. What matters is not absolute efficiency but opportunity cost, the value of what must be given up in order to produce something.

By specializing in goods with lower opportunity costs and trading for the rest, both countries can consume more than they could alone. The theory, first formalized by David Ricardo in the early nineteenth century, helps explain why nations trade extensively even with partners that are less productive overall.

However, the theory makes simplifying assumptions. It assumes that workers can move easily from one industry to another, but in reality a laid-off textile worker may need years of retraining. As a result, the gains from trade are real but unevenly distributed, and some groups can lose even when the nation as a whole gains. This is why trade policy often includes support for displaced workers.

qs.q: According to the passage, what determines comparative advantage?
qs.explain: The passage says what matters is opportunity cost, not absolute efficiency.

qs.q: The word "formalized" in the passage is closest in meaning to
choices: expressed in a precise, systematic way
qs.explain: Ricardo gave the idea a precise, theoretical form.

qs.q: Why does the author mention a laid-off textile worker?
choices: To prove that trade creates no benefits
To explain how wheat is produced
To show that one assumption of the theory may not hold in reality
To show that cloth is less valuable than wheat
qs.explain: The example illustrates that workers cannot always move easily between industries.

qs.q: What can be inferred from the passage about a country that is less productive in every industry?
choices: It will have lower wages than any partner
It can still gain from trading
qs.explain: The theory explains gains from trade even with partners that are more productive overall.

qs.q: According to the passage, why can some groups lose from trade?
choices: Trade lowers the total output of a country
Opportunity costs are the same for all countries
Workers may be unable to move quickly into other industries
qs.explain: The passage ties uneven gains to the difficulty of changing industries.

title: Why Venus Is So Hot
text:
Venus is similar to the Earth in size and composition, yet its surface is hot enough to melt lead. The difference is its atmosphere. Venus is surrounded by a thick layer of carbon dioxide, with pressure at the surface about ninety times that on Earth. Sunlight passes through the clouds and warms the ground, but the heat cannot easily escape back into space, a process known as the greenhouse effect. As a result, the average temperature is about 465 degrees Celsius, hotter than that of Mercury, even though Mercury is much closer to the Sun.

Scientists think Venus may once have had oceans. Computer models suggest that as the young Sun grew brighter, water evaporated and rose into the atmosphere, where ultraviolet light split water molecules apart. The light hydrogen escaped to space, and with it the planet lost the water needed to absorb carbon dioxide into rock. Carbon dioxide from volcanoes then accumulated, intensifying heating.

Studying Venus therefore offers a warning and a lesson. It shows how powerful the greenhouse effect can be and helps researchers judge which planets beyond our solar system might be able to support liquid water.

qs.q: According to the passage, why is Venus hotter than Mercury?
choices: It is closer to the Sun
Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat
It has volcanoes that heat the surface
qs.explain: The greenhouse effect of the thick atmosphere explains the heat despite Mercury being closer to the Sun.

qs.q: The word "accumulated" in the passage is closest in meaning to
qs.explain: Carbon dioxide accumulated means it built up over time.

qs.q: What happened to the hydrogen released when water molecules split?
qs.explain: The passage says the light hydrogen escaped to space.

qs.q: Why does the author mention Mercury?
choices: To argue that Mercury has a thicker atmosphere
To explain how Venus lost its water
To compare the sizes of two planets
To show that distance from the Sun does not alone determine temperature
qs.explain: Venus is hotter though Mercury is much closer to the Sun, so atmosphere matters more than distance.

qs.q: What can be inferred about the early oceans of Venus?
choices: If they had remained, they could have helped remove carbon dioxide from the air
They are still present beneath the clouds
They were caused by volcanic activity
They made the planet hotter than Mercury
qs.explain: Losing water removed the means of absorbing carbon dioxide into rock, implying oceans would have helped.

title: Pidgins and Creoles
text:
When speakers of different languages must communicate regularly without a shared tongue, they often develop a pidgin, a simplified system of communication with a small vocabulary and little grammar. Pidgins are typically no one's native language; they arise in trade settings or on plantations and are learned as a second language for limited purposes. Their vocabulary is usually borrowed from a dominant language, while the sentence structure may owe more to the other languages involved.

A pidgin can undergo a dramatic change if children grow up hearing it as their main input. These children do not merely copy the simplified speech. Instead, they expand it into a creole, a full language with a larger vocabulary, consistent verb markers, and the ability to express complex ideas. Linguists have noted that creoles in different regions, though based on different languages, share some structural similarities, which some scholars see as evidence of an innate human capacity for language.

The idea is contested. Other researchers contend that the similarities result from the shared linguistic backgrounds of the original speakers, not from universal biological programming. Still, all agree that creoles show how quickly a new language can emerge, sometimes within a single generation.

qs.q: According to the passage, where do pidgins typically arise?
choices: Among children who speak the same language
In schools that teach a second language
In settings such as trade or plantations where people lack a common language
In communities with a long written tradition
qs.explain: Pidgins arise in trade settings or on plantations among speakers without a shared language.

qs.q: The word "contested" in the passage is closest in meaning to
qs.explain: The following sentence presents researchers who disagree, so the idea is disputed.

qs.q: Why does the author discuss children who grow up hearing a pidgin?
choices: They forget the pidgin as adults
They prevent the pidgin from spreading
They turn the pidgin into a creole by expanding it
They are the only people who speak dominant languages
qs.explain: The children do not just copy the pidgin; they expand it into a full language.

qs.q: On which point do all researchers mentioned in the passage agree?
choices: A new language can emerge very quickly
Creole similarities prove an innate language capacity
Creoles borrow nothing from other languages
qs.explain: The final sentence says all agree creoles show how quickly new languages can emerge.

qs.q: All of the following are true of pidgins EXCEPT:
choices: They are often learned for limited purposes
Their vocabulary often comes from a dominant language
They are usually learned by children as a first language
qs.explain: Pidgins are typically no one's native language; the other statements are in the passage.

title: The Urban Heat Island
text:
Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon called the urban heat island effect. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and roofing absorb sunlight during the day and release the heat slowly at night, so urban areas cool less after sunset. Buildings also block wind, and cars, air conditioners, and factories add waste heat. Meanwhile, the loss of trees and open soil reduces the cooling that comes from evaporation of water from leaves and ground.

The consequences extend beyond discomfort. Higher temperatures increase electricity demand for cooling, which can strain power grids during heat waves, and they worsen air pollution by speeding the chemical reactions that produce smog. Elderly residents and people without air conditioning face the greatest health risks.

Planners are testing several remedies. Light-colored "cool roofs" reflect more sunlight, and planting trees along streets provides both shade and evaporative cooling. Some cities have also painted roads with reflective coatings, although early trials suggest that the coatings can wear off quickly and may increase glare for drivers. No single strategy works everywhere, so most experts recommend combining several measures.

qs.q: Why do cities cool less than the countryside at night?
choices: Dark surfaces release absorbed heat slowly
qs.explain: The passage says asphalt and roofing absorb heat by day and release it slowly at night.

qs.q: The word "strain" in the passage is closest in meaning to
qs.explain: Strain here means to burden the power grids with excess demand.

qs.q: Why does the author mention reflective road coatings?
choices: To give an example of a remedy with drawbacks
To show that roads cause heat islands
To prove that cool roofs do not work
To explain why trees are unnecessary
qs.explain: The coatings are presented as a remedy that may wear off and cause glare.

qs.q: Which of the following does the passage NOT list as contributing to the urban heat island?
choices: Loss of vegetation and open soil
qs.explain: The passage says buildings block wind, not that wind increases.

qs.q: Why do most experts recommend combining several measures?
choices: Tree planting makes cool roofs unnecessary
No single strategy works in every place
qs.explain: The final sentences say no single strategy works everywhere.

title: Fungal Networks in Forests
text:
Beneath a forest floor lies a web of fungal threads that connect the roots of many trees. These associations, known as mycorrhizae, are a form of symbiosis in which both partners benefit. The fungus extends the reach of the tree's roots, helping it absorb water and minerals such as phosphorus, while the tree supplies the fungus with sugars produced by photosynthesis. Without such partners, many plants would grow poorly in nutrient-poor soil.

In the 1990s, researchers reported that carbon labeled with a radioactive tag moved between neighboring trees of different species through these fungal links. Some scientists interpreted this as evidence that large "mother trees" nurture seedlings, and the idea quickly became popular beyond science. More recent reviews, however, caution that the transferred amounts are small, and there is little evidence that seedlings survive better because of them. Fungi may simply be keeping the carbon for themselves, and different species of fungi may behave very differently.

Even so, no one doubts the importance of mycorrhizae. Experiments consistently show that seedlings grown with the appropriate fungi are larger and healthier than those grown without. The open question is how much, and in what circumstances, resources actually flow from one tree to another.

qs.q: What does the tree provide to the fungus?
qs.explain: The tree supplies sugars; the fungus supplies water and minerals.

qs.q: The word "caution" in the passage is closest in meaning to
qs.explain: Reviews that caution are warning against overstating the evidence.

qs.q: What do recent reviews conclude about carbon transfer between trees?
choices: The amounts are small and the benefit to seedlings is poorly supported
It benefits seedlings more than any other process
It occurs only within a single species
It proves that mother trees exist
qs.explain: The reviews report small transfers and little evidence of improved seedling survival.

qs.q: With which statement would the author most likely agree?
choices: The mother-tree idea has been completely disproved
The mother-tree idea is not yet well supported by evidence
Mycorrhizae are of little importance to plants
Recent reviews confirm that seedlings are nurtured by large trees
qs.explain: The author reports weak evidence but leaves the question open; "completely disproved" goes too far.

qs.q: Why does the author mention seedlings grown with and without fungi?
choices: To prove that carbon moves between trees
To show that mycorrhizae matter even if resource sharing is uncertain
To argue that fungi harm seedlings
To explain how radioactive tags work
qs.explain: The experiments support the fungi's importance independent of the disputed sharing.

title: Perspective in Renaissance Painting
text:
Before the fifteenth century, European painters generally did not try to create realistic depth. Figures were arranged on a flat surface, and their size usually indicated importance rather than distance: a saint might be drawn much larger than the people around him. Around 1420, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated a method that changed this. He painted a view of a building in Florence and asked viewers to look at it through a small hole in the painting while holding a mirror in front of it, so that the painted image could be compared with the real scene.

The method, now called linear perspective, relies on the fact that parallel lines, such as the edges of a road, appear to converge toward a single vanishing point on the horizon. Objects closer to the viewer are drawn larger, and those farther away smaller, in proportion. Leon Battista Alberti described the technique in writing in 1435, which allowed painters across Italy to learn it without meeting Brunelleschi.

Perspective did not make paintings better by itself, and some later artists deliberately distorted it for emotional effect. Nevertheless, it gave painters a mathematical framework for representing space, and it dominated Western art for roughly five hundred years.

qs.q: How did painters before the fifteenth century usually show that a figure was important?
choices: By placing it near the horizon
By painting it in a mirror
qs.explain: The passage says size usually indicated importance, not distance.

qs.q: The word "converge" in the passage is closest in meaning to
qs.explain: Parallel lines appearing to converge meet at a vanishing point.

qs.q: Why does the author mention Alberti?
choices: His writing helped the technique spread across Italy
He painted the first view of Florence
qs.explain: Alberti's 1435 description let painters learn perspective without meeting Brunelleschi.

qs.q: What was the purpose of the mirror in Brunelleschi's demonstration?
choices: To let viewers compare the painting with the real scene
To reflect light onto the saint
qs.explain: The mirror allowed the painted image to be compared with the real building.

qs.q: Which of the following is NOT stated about linear perspective?
choices: Parallel lines appear to converge in it
It lasted in Western art for about five hundred years
It automatically improved the quality of every painting that used it
qs.explain: The author says perspective did not make paintings better by itself.
